properties.title: Territory of Tepic (1884)
properties.label: Territory of Tepic
properties.description: The old seventh canton of Jalisco, where Manuel Lozada's largely indigenous movement had held out against Guadalajara and Mexico City until 1873, was ruled as a military district from 1867 and made a federal territory in 1884. Governed directly from the capital, it became the state of Nayarit under the 1917 Constitution.
properties.note: Drawn from the modern state of Nayarit, which descends from the territory; small boundary changes with Jalisco since then are ignored. Dated to President Manuel González's decree of 12 December 1884.

sources.citation: Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Friedrich Katz, "The Liberal Republic and the Porfiriato, 1867–1910", in Leslie Bethell (ed.), The Cambridge History of Latin America, vol. V (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Wikipedia, "Tepic Territory".

properties.title: Territory of Quintana Roo (1902)
properties.label: Quintana Roo
properties.description: After the army occupied Chan Santa Cruz in 1901, a constitutional amendment of 24 November 1902 took the eastern half of the peninsula from Yucatán and made it a federal territory under military government. It opened the forests to chicle and timber concessions and served as a penal colony; Yucatán's planters resented the loss.
properties.note: Drawn from the modern state of Quintana Roo. The 1902 line with Yucatán and Campeche was disputed and has been adjusted since, so the western edge is only approximate. The territory was abolished in 1931 and restored in 1935 (not mapped).

sources.citation: Nelson A. Reed, The Caste War of Yucatán, rev. ed. (Stanford University Press, 2001).
Allen Wells, Yucatán's Gilded Age: Haciendas, Henequen, and International Harvester, 1860–1915 (University of New Mexico Press, 1985).
H. Congreso del Estado de Quintana Roo, XIII Legislatura, acuerdo reciting the reform of constitutional arts. 43 and 45 of 24 November 1902.

properties.title: Mexico–Guatemala boundary treaty (1882)
properties.label: Guatemala boundary 1882
properties.description: By the treaty of 1882 Guatemala gave up its claims to Chiapas and Soconusco. The line ran along the Suchiate River, past the Tacaná volcano, by straight lines across the highlands, down the Usumacinta, and by a parallel and a meridian around the northern Petén to latitude 17°49′. Surveyed by joint commissions from 1883 to the late 1890s, it is still the border, and it secured the Soconusco, where coffee planting boomed in the following decades.
properties.note: Drawn from the modern border (Natural Earth 1:10m), which follows the line surveyed under the treaty; no later treaty has changed the land line. The river sections follow the modern channels.

sources.citation: Treaty on the delimitation of the frontier between Mexico and Guatemala, signed at Mexico City, 27 September 1882 (Mariscal–Herrera), in force 1 May 1883 (UN Delimitation Treaties Infobase).
Thomas Benjamin, A Rich Land, a Poor People: Politics and Society in Modern Chiapas (University of New Mexico Press, 1989).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).

properties.title: Mexico–British Honduras boundary treaty (1893)
properties.label: Belize boundary 1893
properties.description: Mexico recognised the British colony of British Honduras, and the two governments fixed the boundary from the Boca de Bacalar Chico through Chetumal Bay and up the Río Hondo and Blue Creek to the Guatemalan line; Britain undertook to stop the sale of arms to the rebel Maya. Ratified in 1897, the treaty prepared the way for the Mexican campaign against Chan Santa Cruz.
properties.note: Drawn from the modern land border (Natural Earth 1:10m), from the mouth of the Río Hondo up the river and Blue Creek, then south along the meridian of Garbutt's Falls to the Guatemalan tripoint at 17°49′. The treaty line through Chetumal Bay to the Boca de Bacalar Chico is not drawn.

sources.citation: Treaty between Mexico and Great Britain respecting the boundary between Mexico and British Honduras, signed at Mexico City, 8 July 1893 (Mariscal–St John), with the additional convention of 7 April 1897 (Mariscal–Dering).
Nelson A. Reed, The Caste War of Yucatán, rev. ed. (Stanford University Press, 2001).
Wikipedia, "Belize–Mexico border".

properties.title: Mexican Railway: Veracruz–Mexico City (1873)
properties.label: Mexican Railway
properties.description: Built under concessions going back to the 1830s, with a first stretch out of Veracruz opened in 1850, the line was completed by the London-registered Imperial Mexican Railway company (later the Mexican Railway) and inaugurated by Lerdo. It climbed from the coast through Córdoba and Orizaba and up the Cumbres de Maltrata to the plateau, then crossed the plains of Puebla and Tlaxcala by Apizaco and Apan to the capital. For the first time the journey from the port to Mexico City, which had taken days by coach, could be made in a day.
properties.note: Alignment follows the Natural Earth 1:10m railroads (modern lines, which largely follow the Porfirian ones), routed through Paso del Macho, Córdoba, Fortín, Orizaba, Maltrata, Boca del Monte, Esperanza, Huamantla, Apizaco, Apan, Otumba and Teotihuacán and simplified; at this scale it can be off by a kilometre or more. The Apan–Otumba–Teotihuacán section is drawn station to station. Dated to the inauguration; the Apizaco–Puebla branch is not drawn.

sources.citation: Fred Wilson Powell, The Railroads of Mexico (Stratford Company, 1921).
John H. Coatsworth, Growth Against Development: The Economic Impact of Railroads in Porfirian Mexico (Northern Illinois University Press, 1981).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 12.

properties.title: Sonora Railway: Guaymas–Nogales (1882)
properties.label: Sonora Railway
properties.description: Built by the Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe between 1879 and 1882, the line linked the port of Guaymas through Hermosillo to the US border at Nogales, where it met the line from Benson, Arizona, on 25 October 1882. It connected Sonora to the US network before Sonora had any rail link with central Mexico, and tied the northwest's mines and farms to Arizona and California.
properties.note: Alignment follows the Natural Earth 1:10m railroads (modern lines, which largely follow the Porfirian ones), routed through Hermosillo and simplified; at this scale it can be off by a kilometre or more.

sources.citation: David M. Pletcher, Rails, Mines, and Progress: Seven American Promoters in Mexico, 1867–1911 (Cornell University Press, 1958).
Fred Wilson Powell, The Railroads of Mexico (Stratford Company, 1921).
Union Pacific, "Nogales, Arizona" (Train Town history).
Sonora Railway records, finding aid (Online Archive of California).

properties.title: Mexican Central Railway: Mexico City–Paso del Norte (1884)
properties.label: Mexican Central
properties.description: The Boston-financed Mexican Central roughly paralleled the old Camino Real de Tierra Adentro through Querétaro, the Bajío towns, Aguascalientes and Zacatecas, then struck north across the Laguna to Chihuahua and Paso del Norte, where it met the US railways at El Paso. The first through train from Mexico City reached Paso del Norte on 25 March 1884. It was the backbone of the Porfirian network and bound the north to both Mexico City and the United States.
properties.note: Alignment follows the Natural Earth 1:10m railroads (modern lines, which largely follow the Porfirian ones), routed through Tula, San Juan del Río, Querétaro, Celaya, Irapuato, Silao, León, Lagos de Moreno, Aguascalientes, Zacatecas, Fresnillo, Cañitas, Camacho, Torreón, Jiménez and Chihuahua and simplified; at this scale it can be off by a kilometre or more. The Zacatecas–Fresnillo–Cañitas section is drawn station to station. Dated to the month of the first through train (Kuntz Ficker); a commonly cited last-spike date of 8 March 1884 was not confirmed.

sources.citation: Sandra Kuntz Ficker, Empresa extranjera y mercado interno: el Ferrocarril Central Mexicano, 1880–1907 (El Colegio de México, 1995).
John H. Coatsworth, Growth Against Development: The Economic Impact of Railroads in Porfirian Mexico (Northern Illinois University Press, 1981).
Fred Wilson Powell, The Railroads of Mexico (Stratford Company, 1921).

properties.title: Mexican Central: Irapuato–Guadalajara branch (1888)
properties.label: Guadalajara branch
properties.description: The branch from Irapuato along the Lerma valley by La Piedad and Ocotlán linked Guadalajara, Mexico's second city, to the national network; it was later extended toward the Pacific at Manzanillo.
properties.note: Alignment follows the Natural Earth 1:10m railroads (modern lines, which largely follow the Porfirian ones), routed through La Piedad and Ocotlán and simplified; at this scale it can be off by a kilometre or more.

sources.citation: Sandra Kuntz Ficker, Empresa extranjera y mercado interno: el Ferrocarril Central Mexicano, 1880–1907 (El Colegio de México, 1995).
Fred Wilson Powell, The Railroads of Mexico (Stratford Company, 1921).

properties.title: Guadalajara–Manzanillo railway (1908)
properties.label: Manzanillo line
properties.description: A short line from Manzanillo to Colima by Armería opened on 16 September 1889 and was bought by the Mexican Central in 1905. The Central's line south from Guadalajara by Zapotlán (Ciudad Guzmán) down through the barrancas to Colima, among the hardest sections of the Porfirian system to build, completed the link in 1908 and gave the network an outlet on the Pacific.
properties.note: Alignment follows the Natural Earth 1:10m railroads (modern lines, which largely follow the Porfirian ones), routed through Ciudad Guzmán and Colima and simplified; at this scale it can be off by a kilometre or more. The Colima–Armería–Manzanillo section is drawn station to station. Dated to the completion of the through line; the Colima–Manzanillo section is older (1889).

sources.citation: Fred Wilson Powell, The Railroads of Mexico (Stratford Company, 1921).
Sandra Kuntz Ficker, Empresa extranjera y mercado interno: el Ferrocarril Central Mexicano, 1880–1907 (El Colegio de México, 1995).
H. Congreso del Estado de Colima, history of the XI Legislatura (1889).

properties.title: Mexican National Railway: Mexico City–Nuevo Laredo (1888)
properties.label: Mexican National
properties.description: A narrow-gauge line built by the Palmer–Sullivan concession, it ran west from the capital by Toluca and Acámbaro, then north through Celaya, San Miguel de Allende, San Luis Potosí, Saltillo and Monterrey to the border at Nuevo Laredo. It gave the northeast, and Monterrey's rising industries, the shortest route to the Texas railways; it was converted to standard gauge in 1903.
properties.note: Alignment follows the Natural Earth 1:10m railroads (modern lines, which largely follow the Porfirian ones), routed through Toluca, Maravatío, Acámbaro, Celaya, San Miguel de Allende, San Luis Potosí, Saltillo and Monterrey and simplified; at this scale it can be off by a kilometre or more, and the modern line passes about 6 km from central Saltillo. The Mexico City terminus was the Colonia station, about a kilometre from Buenavista. The later Querétaro cut-off is not drawn. Dated to the completion of the through line in September 1888 (Wikipedia); Kuntz Ficker has the line working from early 1888.

sources.citation: David M. Pletcher, Rails, Mines, and Progress: Seven American Promoters in Mexico, 1867–1911 (Cornell University Press, 1958).
John H. Coatsworth, Growth Against Development: The Economic Impact of Railroads in Porfirian Mexico (Northern Illinois University Press, 1981).
Fred Wilson Powell, The Railroads of Mexico (Stratford Company, 1921).
Wikipedia, "National Railroad of Mexico".

properties.title: Mexican International Railroad: Piedras Negras–Torreón–Durango (1888–1892)
properties.label: Mexican International
properties.description: Backed by the Southern Pacific, the International ran from the border at Ciudad Porfirio Díaz (Piedras Negras) past the Sabinas coalfields and Monclova to Torreón, reached in 1888, and on to Durango in October 1892. Coal from Coahuila and the meeting with the Mexican Central at Torreón made the Laguna a railway crossroads.
properties.note: Alignment follows the Natural Earth 1:10m railroads (modern lines, which largely follow the Porfirian ones), routed through Sabinas, Monclova, San Pedro de las Colonias and Torreón and simplified; at this scale it can be off by a kilometre or more. The Monclova–San Pedro section (about 200 km) is drawn station to station because no matching modern line is in the reference data, and it is not confirmed that the line passed through San Pedro, so that section is schematic. The line reached Sabinas in December 1883 and met the Central at Torreón in March 1888.

sources.citation: John H. Coatsworth, Growth Against Development: The Economic Impact of Railroads in Porfirian Mexico (Northern Illinois University Press, 1981).
Fred Wilson Powell, The Railroads of Mexico (Stratford Company, 1921).
William K. Meyers, Forge of Progress, Crucible of Revolt: Origins of the Mexican Revolution in La Comarca Lagunera, 1880–1911 (University of New Mexico Press, 1994).

properties.title: Mexican Central: Tampico branch (1890)
properties.label: Tampico branch
properties.description: From Chicalote near Aguascalientes the branch ran east through San Luis Potosí and down the Sierra Madre Oriental by Cárdenas and the Tamasopo canyon to the Gulf at Tampico, giving the Central its own port. Two decades later Tampico became the shipping point of the oil boom.
properties.note: Alignment follows the Natural Earth 1:10m railroads (modern lines, which largely follow the Porfirian ones), routed through San Luis Potosí and Cárdenas and simplified; at this scale it can be off by a kilometre or more. The Chicalote–San Luis Potosí section is drawn station to station. Dated 1890 (Wikipedia); Kuntz Ficker gives 1889 for the start of service.

sources.citation: Sandra Kuntz Ficker, Empresa extranjera y mercado interno: el Ferrocarril Central Mexicano, 1880–1907 (El Colegio de México, 1995).
Fred Wilson Powell, The Railroads of Mexico (Stratford Company, 1921).

properties.title: Interoceanic Railway: Mexico City–Puebla–Jalapa–Veracruz (1891)
properties.label: Interoceanic
properties.description: A British company formed in 1888 took over earlier local lines, among them Puebla–San Martín Texmelucan (1882), and completed a narrow-gauge rival to the Mexican Railway in 1891. It ran from San Lázaro station in Mexico City by Ayotla and Río Frío to San Martín and Puebla, then across the highlands by Perote and down to the coast through Jalapa, giving Puebla and Jalapa a second line between the capital and Veracruz.
properties.note: Alignment follows the Natural Earth 1:10m railroads (modern lines, which largely follow the Porfirian ones), routed through Puebla, Perote and Jalapa and simplified; at this scale it can be off by a kilometre or more. The Mexico City–Ayotla–Río Frío–San Martín–Puebla section is drawn station to station. Sources disagree on whether Puebla was a main-line station from the start, and the stations between Puebla and Perote are not established here, so the whole line is marked schematic.

sources.citation: Fred Wilson Powell, The Railroads of Mexico (Stratford Company, 1921).
John H. Coatsworth, Growth Against Development: The Economic Impact of Railroads in Porfirian Mexico (Northern Illinois University Press, 1981).
Wikipedia, "Interoceanic Railway of Mexico".
Eumed.net, "La estación de San Martín Texmelucan" (history of the Puebla–San Martín line and the Interoceanic).

properties.title: Mexican Southern Railway: Puebla–Oaxaca (1892)
properties.label: Mexican Southern
properties.description: Built for a British company by the contractors Read & Campbell, the narrow-gauge line ran from Puebla through Tehuacán (reached in 1891) and the Tomellín canyon to Oaxaca City, where Díaz opened it in November 1892. It ended the isolation of his home state from the capital.
properties.note: Alignment follows the Natural Earth 1:10m railroads (modern lines, which largely follow the Porfirian ones), routed through Tehuacán and simplified; at this scale it can be off by a kilometre or more.

sources.citation: Fred Wilson Powell, The Railroads of Mexico (Stratford Company, 1921).
Friedrich Katz, "The Liberal Republic and the Porfiriato, 1867–1910", in Leslie Bethell (ed.), The Cambridge History of Latin America, vol. V (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Wikipedia, "Mexican Southern Railroad".

properties.title: Tehuantepec Railway: Coatzacoalcos–Salina Cruz (1907)
properties.label: Tehuantepec Railway
properties.description: A line across the isthmus had been completed in 1894 but was barely usable. Rebuilt by Pearson in partnership with the government, with new harbours at Coatzacoalcos (Puerto México) and Salina Cruz, it was reopened by Díaz in January 1907 and for a few years carried a large share of the transit trade between the Atlantic and Pacific, until the Panama Canal opened in 1914.
properties.note: Alignment follows the Natural Earth 1:10m railroads (modern lines, which largely follow the Porfirian ones), routed through the two terminals and simplified; at this scale it can be off by a kilometre or more. Sources give 23 or 25 January 1907 for the formal reopening, so it is dated to the month.

sources.citation: Paul Garner, British Lions and Mexican Eagles: Business, Politics, and Empire in the Career of Weetman Pearson in Mexico, 1889–1919 (Stanford University Press, 2011).
Fred Wilson Powell, The Railroads of Mexico (Stratford Company, 1921).
Wikipedia, "Tehuantepec Railway".
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 13.

properties.title: Mérida–Progreso railway (1881)
properties.label: Mérida–Progreso
properties.description: The short line from Mérida to the port of Progreso was the first of a dense web of Yucatecan railways built by planters to move henequen from the haciendas to the ships. Progreso, which replaced Sisal as the peninsula's port, shipped almost all of the fibre to the United States.
properties.note: Alignment follows the Natural Earth 1:10m railroads (modern lines, which largely follow the Porfirian ones), routed through the two terminals and simplified; at this scale it can be off by a kilometre or more.

sources.citation: Allen Wells, Yucatán's Gilded Age: Haciendas, Henequen, and International Harvester, 1860–1915 (University of New Mexico Press, 1985).
INAH, Lugares, "Ferrocarril Mérida–Progreso" (inaugurated 15 September 1881).

properties.title: Ferrocarriles Nacionales de México formed
properties.label: National Railways 1908
properties.description: Worried that US railroad combinations would control Mexico's trunk lines, Finance Minister José Yves Limantour merged the Mexican Central and the National into a new company in which the government held a majority. By 1910 the country had roughly 19,000 km of track, against about 600 km in 1876.
properties.note: Marked at Buenavista, the Mexico City terminus of the Mexican Central and the Mexican Railway. The agreement was signed in February 1908; the new company took over the National's lines in January 1909 and the Central's in February 1909.

sources.citation: John H. Coatsworth, Growth Against Development: The Economic Impact of Railroads in Porfirian Mexico (Northern Illinois University Press, 1981).
Paul Garner, Porfirio Díaz (Longman, 2001).
Friedrich Katz, "The Liberal Republic and the Porfiriato, 1867–1910", in Leslie Bethell (ed.), The Cambridge History of Latin America, vol. V (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 12–13.

properties.title: Victorio killed at Tres Castillos
properties.label: Tres Castillos
properties.description: Chihuahuan forces under Joaquín Terrazas trapped the Apache leader Victorio and his band at the hills of Tres Castillos and killed him with most of his warriors. With Geronimo's surrender in Arizona in 1886, it largely ended the Apache raiding that had devastated Chihuahua and Sonora for half a century, and opened the northern ranges to railways, ranching and mining.
properties.note: Marked at the hills of Tres Castillos, from the coordinate given by Wikipedia (29°58′N, 105°47′W), in the desert northeast of Chihuahua City; the locality of Tres Castillos (Coyame del Sotol) lies about 16 km to the south. Sources give 14 or 15 October.

sources.citation: Dan L. Thrapp, Victorio and the Mimbres Apaches (University of Oklahoma Press, 1974).
Friedrich Katz, "The Liberal Republic and the Porfiriato, 1867–1910", in Leslie Bethell (ed.), The Cambridge History of Latin America, vol. V (Cambridge University Press, 1986).

properties.title: Tomóchic rebellion
properties.label: Tomóchic
properties.description: Villagers of Tomóchic in the Sierra Tarahumara, inspired by the healer Teresa Urrea, the "Saint of Cabora", refused the authority of state and church officials and twice defeated federal troops. In October 1892 a large army besieged the village and destroyed it, killing nearly all its defenders. The episode became a symbol of the regime's brutality in the sierra.
properties.note: Marked at the modern village of Tomochi (municipality of Guerrero, Chihuahua). Gillingham (ch. 12, from the army's own returns) gives 1,200 troops in the final assault, 217 defenders killed and 114 survivors, nearly all women and girls, marched away; he calls Teresa Urrea "Santa Teresa de Cabora".

sources.citation: Paul J. Vanderwood, The Power of God against the Guns of Government: Religious Upheaval in Mexico at the Turn of the Nineteenth Century (Stanford University Press, 1998).
Friedrich Katz, "The Liberal Republic and the Porfiriato, 1867–1910", in Leslie Bethell (ed.), The Cambridge History of Latin America, vol. V (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 12.

properties.title: Cananea strike
properties.label: Cananea
properties.description: Mexican miners at William C. Greene's Cananea Consolidated Copper Company struck for a five-peso, eight-hour day and the same treatment as American workers. Fighting broke out, and the governor of Sonora let a party of armed Arizona volunteers cross the border from Naco to help suppress the strike. The leaders, linked to the Liberal Party of the Flores Magón brothers, were jailed in San Juan de Ulúa.
properties.note: Gillingham (ch. 13) dates the strike to 1907 and says 23 miners were shot by company guards and Arizona Rangers; the strike was in June 1906, and the Arizona volunteers were led by the Arizona Ranger captain Thomas Rynning.

sources.citation: Rodney D. Anderson, Outcasts in Their Own Land: Mexican Industrial Workers, 1906–1911 (Northern Illinois University Press, 1976).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, vol. 1: Porfirians, Liberals and Peasants (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 13.

properties.title: Liberal Party risings of 1906 (Acayucan)
properties.label: Acayucan 1906
properties.description: The Liberal Party junta of Ricardo Flores Magón, exiled in the United States, planned a series of armed risings against Díaz for the autumn of 1906. A small band briefly took Jiménez, Coahuila, on 26 September, and on the night of 30 September Hilario C. Salas led an attack on Acayucan in southern Veracruz that collapsed when he was wounded. Other planned risings were broken up by arrests, but the attempts foreshadowed the armed opposition of 1910–11.
properties.note: Marked at the town of Acayucan; the rebels gathered in the surrounding sierra. Jiménez, Coahuila, on the Rio Grande, is not marked separately. The number of rebels at Acayucan is given variously, from about three hundred to over a thousand.

sources.citation: James D. Cockcroft, Intellectual Precursors of the Mexican Revolution, 1900–1913 (University of Texas Press, 1968).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, vol. 1: Porfirians, Liberals and Peasants (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Wikipedia, "Acayucan Rebellion".
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 14.

properties.title: Deportation of the Yaquis to Yucatán (1902–1908)
properties.label: Yaqui deportations
properties.description: To break Yaqui resistance to the surveying and sale of their river valley, the governments of Díaz and the Sonoran governors deported thousands of Yaqui men, women and children, peaking in 1907–08. Many were shipped from Guaymas to San Blas, marched overland to the railhead at San Marcos, Jalisco, taken by train through Guadalajara and Mexico City to Veracruz, and shipped to Progreso to be sold as labourers to the henequen haciendas of Yucatán, where many died. Families were split up on the way.
properties.note: Schematic route following the stages described by Turner (1910): by government ship from Guaymas to San Blas, on foot via Tepic to San Marcos, by the Mexican Central via Guadalajara to Mexico City, by rail to Veracruz, by sea to Progreso and on to Mérida. The Tepic–San Marcos leg is drawn by Ixtlán, on the road between them; Ixtlán is not named by Turner. Turner calls the Mexico City–Veracruz line the "International"; which line was used is not established, so that leg is drawn straight. Other deportees went by different routes and to other destinations; the dates and stages varied.

sources.citation: Evelyn Hu-DeHart, Yaqui Resistance and Survival: The Struggle for Land and Autonomy, 1821–1910 (University of Wisconsin Press, 1984).
John Kenneth Turner, Barbarous Mexico (Charles H. Kerr & Company, 1910).
John Kenneth Turner, Barbarous Mexico (Charles H. Kerr & Company, 1910), ch. 3, "The Tragedy of the Yaquis" (Wikisource).
Raquel Padilla Ramos, "De una luxación coxofemoral a la autopsia 642. Bioética y práctica médica sobre cuerpos yaquis en Yucatán porfiriano", Noroeste de México, nueva época, no. 1 (INAH, 2020).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 12.

properties.title: Fundidora de Monterrey
properties.label: Fundidora
properties.description: The Compañía Fundidora de Fierro y Acero de Monterrey, founded in 1900 by Monterrey merchants and foreign partners, was Latin America's first integrated iron and steel works; its first blast furnace was lit in 1903. With the Cuauhtémoc brewery (1890), glassworks and smelters, it made Monterrey, served by the railways to Laredo, Tampico and the Laguna, the industrial capital of the north.
properties.note: Marked at the steelworks site, now Parque Fundidora.

sources.citation: Alex M. Saragoza, The Monterrey Elite and the Mexican State, 1880–1940 (University of Texas Press, 1988).
Friedrich Katz, "The Liberal Republic and the Porfiriato, 1867–1910", in Leslie Bethell (ed.), The Cambridge History of Latin America, vol. V (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 12.

properties.title: Torreón and the Laguna cotton boom
properties.label: Torreón / La Laguna
properties.description: Torreón grew from a ranch where the Mexican Central (1883) and the Mexican International (1888) crossed into a city by 1907. Around it, the floodwaters of the Nazas irrigated cotton estates that supplied the national textile industry, drawing tens of thousands of migrant workers; disputes over the river's water and the region's labour made the Laguna a centre of the coming revolution.
properties.note: Marked at Torreón; the cotton district of the Comarca Lagunera spreads across Coahuila and Durango around the city.

sources.citation: William K. Meyers, Forge of Progress, Crucible of Revolt: Origins of the Mexican Revolution in La Comarca Lagunera, 1880–1911 (University of New Mexico Press, 1994).
Friedrich Katz, "The Liberal Republic and the Porfiriato, 1867–1910", in Leslie Bethell (ed.), The Cambridge History of Latin America, vol. V (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 12–13.

properties.title: Black American colony at Tlahualilo
properties.label: Tlahualilo 1895
properties.description: William Henry Ellis, a Texas-born former slave who did business in Mexico as Guillermo Eliseo, contracted with the Tlahualilo cotton company to settle African American families from the US South on its estate in the Laguna. About 800 colonists, most from Alabama, arrived early in 1895, but disease, gang labour and poor conditions broke the colony within months, and most went home with US government help. It was one of many Porfirian colonisation schemes that failed in the north.
properties.note: Marked at Tlahualilo de Zaragoza, Durango, the seat of the Tlahualilo estate; the colonists' camps lay on the estate lands around it. Sources give 816 to about 2,000 emigrants; 816 is the usual figure for the 1895 transfer. Gillingham (ch. 12) has the colony fail inside eight months of 1895.

sources.citation: Karl Jacoby, The Strange Career of William Ellis: The Texas Slave Who Became a Mexican Millionaire (W. W. Norton, 2016).
Wikipedia, "William Henry Ellis (businessman)".
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 12.

properties.title: San José de Gracia founded
properties.label: San José de Gracia
properties.description: Ranchers of the old hacienda of Cojumatlán, in the uplands of northwestern Michoacán, laid out a new village on a grid around a church and plaza. It grew into a prosperous community of cattlemen who sold cheese and leather to Mexico City by way of a railway station some 25 km away, an example of the small-ranch Mexico that did well under Díaz. The historian Luis González y González, who was born there, made it the subject of his microhistory Pueblo en vilo, which Gillingham follows through the Revolution and the Cristero War.
properties.note: Marked at the town, now the seat of the municipality of Marcos Castellanos. Dated to the official founding on 19 March, the feast of St Joseph.
properties.modern_place: San José de Gracia, Marcos Castellanos, Michoacán, Mexico

sources.citation: Luis González y González, San José de Gracia: Mexican Village in Transition, trans. John Upton (University of Texas Press, 1974).
Wikipedia (es), "San José de Gracia (Michoacán)".
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 13.

properties.title: First commercial oil field at Ébano
properties.label: Ébano oil 1904
properties.description: The Californian oilman Edward L. Doheny bought land near Ébano, west of Tampico, and in 1904 his Mexican Petroleum Company brought in the first commercially productive wells in Mexico. Its heavy oil went to fuel locomotives and pave streets, and it began the oil industry of the Huasteca around Tampico.
properties.note: Marked at the town of Ébano; the wells lay in the surrounding Huasteca lowlands. Gillingham (chs. 12, 16) calls Doheny's firm Standard Oil. Doheny's Mexican Petroleum and Huasteca companies were independent until Standard Oil of Indiana bought control of his holding company in 1925; by the 1938 expropriation Huasteca Petroleum belonged to Standard Oil of New Jersey.

sources.citation: Jonathan C. Brown, Oil and Revolution in Mexico (University of California Press, 1993).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 16.

properties.title: Dos Bocas well fire
properties.label: Dos Bocas 1908
properties.description: Pearson's well San Diego de la Mar No. 3 (San Diego del Mar in some sources), near the Tamiahua lagoon in northern Veracruz, blew out, caught fire and burned for nearly two months, leaving two great craters known as Dos Bocas. It was the first great disaster of the Mexican oil industry and proved the richness of the Huasteca fields. Gillingham describes how the companies afterwards pressed local Tének (Huastec) villagers into fighting well fires.
properties.note: Marked at the craters, from the coordinate given by Wikipedia (21°31′34″N, 97°37′58″W), in the municipality of Ozuluama; the town of Ozuluama is about 27 km to the northwest. Estimates of the oil lost range widely; Gillingham (ch. 16) gives a million tons. Sources differ on the well's number.

sources.citation: Jonathan C. Brown, Oil and Revolution in Mexico (University of California Press, 1993).
Myrna I. Santiago, The Ecology of Oil: Environment, Labor, and the Mexican Revolution, 1900–1938 (Cambridge University Press, 2006).
Wikipedia, "Dos Bocas oil fire".
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 16.

properties.title: Potrero del Llano No. 4 and the Golden Lane
properties.label: Potrero del Llano
properties.description: Weetman Pearson's El Águila company struck one of the largest gushers in the world at Potrero del Llano in northern Veracruz, which flowed uncontrolled for weeks. It proved the "Golden Lane", the chain of fields south of Tampico, which made Mexico one of the world's leading oil producers during the Revolution.
properties.note: Marked at the locality of Potrero del Llano (Álamo Temapache, Veracruz). The Golden Lane fields, which run in an arc from near Tampico to Álamo, are not drawn. Some accounts date the strike to 26 December.

sources.citation: Jonathan C. Brown, Oil and Revolution in Mexico (University of California Press, 1993).
Paul Garner, British Lions and Mexican Eagles: Business, Politics, and Empire in the Career of Weetman Pearson in Mexico, 1889–1919 (Stanford University Press, 2011).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 16.

properties.title: Drainage of the Valley of Mexico
properties.label: Gran Canal del Desagüe
properties.description: Díaz inaugurated the Gran Canal del Desagüe, a canal of about 47 km from the eastern edge of Mexico City to a tunnel at Tequixquiac, through which the basin's floodwater finally drained north to the Tula and Pánuco rivers. It completed a project begun in the colonial era, ended the regular flooding of the capital, and with the later pumping of groundwater helped dry out the remaining lakes.
properties.note: Marked at Tequixquiac, near the tunnel through which the canal leaves the basin; the canal itself is not drawn. Gillingham (ch. 13) has Díaz inaugurating the drainage when it was finished in 1905 and again for the 1910 centenary; the canal and tunnel were formally opened on 17 March 1900, and related works (the city sewers, the Xochimilco water supply) went on into the 1900s.

sources.citation: Manuel Perló Cohen, El paradigma porfiriano: historia del desagüe del Valle de México (UNAM / Miguel Ángel Porrúa, 1999).
Paul Garner, British Lions and Mexican Eagles: Business, Politics, and Empire in the Career of Weetman Pearson in Mexico, 1889–1919 (Stanford University Press, 2011).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 12–13.

properties.title: Drainage of the Zacapu marsh (hacienda Cantabria)
properties.label: Zacapu marsh drained
properties.description: With a federal concession obtained through their uncle Íñigo Noriega, the Spanish brothers Eduardo and Alfredo Noriega drained the lake and marsh of Zacapu in northern Michoacán and turned some 12,000 hectares into the maize and wheat fields of their hacienda, Cantabria. The Purépecha villages around the marsh, among them Naranja, Tiríndaro and Tarejero, lost land, fishing and the reeds they wove, and many villagers left as migrant labourers. Naranja became a centre of the agrarian movement of the 1920s.
properties.note: Marked at the locality of Cantabria (Zacapu), the hacienda headquarters; the drained marsh lay between Zacapu and the villages to the south and east. Guzmán Ávila dates the works from 1899 to the last years of the Porfiriato. Gillingham (ch. 12, following Friedrich) names the brothers Íñigo and Remigio Noriega and dates their campaign for the land to 1883; Íñigo Noriega drained Lake Chalco under an 1895 concession, and the archival record has his nephews running Cantabria.

sources.citation: José Napoleón Guzmán Ávila, La ciénega de Zacapu, Michoacán: de la conformación de las haciendas al reparto agrario, 1870–1940 (PhD thesis, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, 2009).
Paul Friedrich, Agrarian Revolt in a Mexican Village (University of Chicago Press, 1977).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 12.

properties.title: Río Blanco strike
properties.label: Río Blanco
properties.description: The textile workers of the large French-owned mill at Río Blanco, near Orizaba, refused to return to work on the terms of an arbitration award by Díaz that ended a lockout across the industry. They burned the tienda de raya that supplied the mill hands, and federal troops crushed the rising, killing many workers. Together with Cananea it showed the regime's readiness to use force against labour.

sources.citation: Rodney D. Anderson, Outcasts in Their Own Land: Mexican Industrial Workers, 1906–1911 (Northern Illinois University Press, 1976).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, vol. 1: Porfirians, Liberals and Peasants (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 13.

properties.title: The Creelman interview
properties.label: Creelman interview
properties.description: At Chapultepec Castle Díaz told the American journalist James Creelman that Mexico was ready for democracy, that he would welcome an opposition party and that he would not serve again after 1910. Translated and reprinted in Mexico, the interview set off a scramble over the succession: supporters of Bernardo Reyes organised, and Francisco Madero published La sucesión presidencial en 1910 and began the campaign that Díaz answered by having him jailed and rigging the 1910 election.
properties.note: Marked at Chapultepec Castle, the presidential residence, where the interview was given early in 1908. Dated to its publication in the March 1908 issue of Pearson's Magazine.
properties.modern_place: Castillo de Chapultepec, Ciudad de México

sources.citation: James Creelman, "President Díaz: Hero of the Americas", Pearson's Magazine 19, no. 3 (March 1908).
Wikipedia, "Creelman interview".
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 13–14.

properties.title: The sugar haciendas of Morelos
properties.label: Morelos sugar
properties.description: With the railway to the capital and new mill machinery, the sugar haciendas of Morelos expanded across the valleys of Cuautla and Cuernavaca, absorbing the fields, water and woodland of the villages. The pressure on village lands here produced the rebellion of Emiliano Zapata in 1911.
properties.note: Marked at Cuautla; the estates covered the lowlands of Morelos. Gillingham (ch. 12) notes that the hacienda of Santa Clara alone enclosed twelve villages and a tenth of the state.

sources.citation: John Womack Jr., Zapata and the Mexican Revolution (Alfred A. Knopf, 1969).
Friedrich Katz, "The Liberal Republic and the Porfiriato, 1867–1910", in Leslie Bethell (ed.), The Cambridge History of Latin America, vol. V (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 12–13.

properties.title: Valle Nacional
properties.label: Valle Nacional
properties.description: In this hot valley of northern Oaxaca, tobacco planters used labourers recruited by deception (enganchados) and petty offenders consigned by jefes políticos, held in debt and under guard. The American journalist John Kenneth Turner, who visited in 1908, made it the emblem of Porfirian forced labour.
properties.note: Marked at San Juan Bautista Valle Nacional. Dated to Turner's visit in late 1908; the system flourished from the 1890s.
properties.modern_place: San Juan Bautista Valle Nacional, Oaxaca, Mexico

sources.citation: John Kenneth Turner, Barbarous Mexico (Charles H. Kerr & Company, 1910).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, vol. 1: Porfirians, Liberals and Peasants (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
John Kenneth Turner, Barbarous Mexico (Charles H. Kerr & Company, 1910), ch. 5 (Wikisource).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 12.

properties.title: Coffee in the Soconusco
properties.label: Soconusco coffee
properties.description: Once the 1882 treaty settled the border, the slopes above Tapachula were sold off to coffee planters, many of them German, and worked by seasonal labourers brought down from the Chiapas highlands and across from Guatemala. The Soconusco became one of Mexico's main export regions.
properties.note: Marked at Tapachula; the plantations lay on the slopes of the Sierra Madre de Chiapas to the north and east.

sources.citation: Thomas Benjamin, A Rich Land, a Poor People: Politics and Society in Modern Chiapas (University of New Mexico Press, 1989).
Friedrich Katz, "The Liberal Republic and the Porfiriato, 1867–1910", in Leslie Bethell (ed.), The Cambridge History of Latin America, vol. V (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 12.

properties.title: The henequen boom
properties.label: Henequen boom
properties.description: Demand for binder twine from the mechanical reapers of the US wheat belt turned the dry northwest of Yucatán into a sea of henequen plantations. The fibre was sold mostly to International Harvester (formed 1902), which bought through the Mérida house of Olegario Molina, while Maya peons, Yaqui deportees and contract labourers worked the haciendas in debt servitude.
properties.note: Marked at Mérida; the henequen zone lay in a belt around the city.

sources.citation: Allen Wells, Yucatán's Gilded Age: Haciendas, Henequen, and International Harvester, 1860–1915 (University of New Mexico Press, 1985).
John Kenneth Turner, Barbarous Mexico (Charles H. Kerr & Company, 1910).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 12.

properties.title: Payo Obispo founded
properties.label: Payo Obispo
properties.description: The naval officer Othón P. Blanco founded Payo Obispo at the mouth of the Río Hondo to enforce the new boundary with British Honduras and cut the arms trade to the rebel Maya. It became the capital of Quintana Roo and is now Chetumal.

sources.citation: Nelson A. Reed, The Caste War of Yucatán, rev. ed. (Stanford University Press, 2001).

properties.title: Federal army occupies Chan Santa Cruz
properties.label: Chan Santa Cruz taken
properties.description: General Ignacio Bravo's army, advancing slowly from Peto and building a road, a telegraph line and forts behind it, entered the rebel Maya capital, which its people had abandoned. The occupation marked the formal end of the Caste War, although Maya villages in the forest stayed beyond effective government control for decades.
properties.modern_place: Felipe Carrillo Puerto, Quintana Roo, Mexico

sources.citation: Nelson A. Reed, The Caste War of Yucatán, rev. ed. (Stanford University Press, 2001).
Pascale Villegas, "Una medalla militar por matar mayas rebeldes (1901–1905)", Estudios de Cultura Maya 50 (2017).

properties.note: Marked at the modern town of Felipe Carrillo Puerto. Bravo's telegram is dated 4 May 1901; some sources give 3 May.

properties.title: The Centenario of Independence
properties.label: Centenario 1910
properties.description: The regime celebrated a hundred years of independence with a month of parades, congresses and inaugurations, among them the Independence column on the Paseo de la Reforma, unveiled on 16 September. The display of order and progress for foreign delegations came months after an election in which Díaz had his opponent Madero jailed.
properties.note: The Independence column (the "Ángel") on the Paseo de la Reforma.
properties.modern_place: Ángel de la Independencia, Ciudad de México

sources.citation: Mauricio Tenorio-Trillo, "1910 Mexico City: Space and Nation in the City of the Centenario", Journal of Latin American Studies 28:1 (1996).
Paul Garner, Porfirio Díaz (Longman, 2001).

properties.title: Plan of San Luis Potosí
properties.label: Plan of San Luis
properties.description: Francisco I. Madero, the Anti-Reelectionist candidate, had been arrested in Monterrey during the 1910 campaign and held at San Luis Potosí while Díaz was declared re-elected. Released on bail, he fled to San Antonio, Texas, where his plan was written and published. Dated 5 October, his last day in San Luis, it declared the election void and called for a rising on 20 November 1910.
properties.note: Marked at San Antonio, Texas, where the plan was drafted and issued; it bears the date and place of San Luis Potosí.

sources.citation: Stanley R. Ross, Francisco I. Madero: Apostle of Mexican Democracy (Columbia University Press, 1955).
Charles C. Cumberland, Mexican Revolution: Genesis under Madero (University of Texas Press, 1952).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, vol. 1: Porfirians, Liberals and Peasants (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 13–14.
